title: Man. Post. Cap. IV: GAR Resp. — privatio activa / passiva
pass_a_gloss: GAR. Reply. About the major I raise no dispute here: it will be disputed below whether violation of a divine precept, which is sin, can be the penalty of sin. To the minor I say that privation of justice must be distinguished, so that we name one active, another passive. Active is that by which the man himself by acting badly strips himself of the justice with which God had endowed him: passive that by which God deprives the man of justice and of the gifts with which he had heaped him. If therefore we acknowledge that active privation of justice is the same as violation of the law, yet of passive privation that will deservedly be denied.
pass_b_english: Garissoles replies. I will not contest the major here; later we can ask whether breaking a divine precept (which is sin) can also be sin's penalty. On the minor I distinguish two privations of righteousness: active and passive. Active is the man's own bad acting by which he strips himself of the righteousness God had given him. Passive is God's stripping the man of that righteousness and of the gifts heaped on him. Grant that the active privation is the same as law-breaking; the passive still is not.
source_text: GAR. Respond. De majore litem hic non moveo: disputabitur inferius, an violatio praecepti divini, quae peccatum est, possit esse poena peccati. Ad minorem dico, distinguendam esse privationem justitiae, ut aliam activam nominemus, aliam passivam. Activa est, qua homo ipse male agendo justitia seipsum spoliat, qua Deus illum impertiverat: passiva qua Deus hominem justitia privat, & donis quibus ipsum cumularat. Si ergo agnoscimus privationem activam justitiae idem esse cum violatione legis; de privatione tamen passiva id merito negabitur.
